extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of logic, philosophy of language, and philosophy of science
extracted.subtask_description: Theory and practical principles for forming and using general names, classes, and definitions (the Aristotelian predicables: genus, species, differentia, proprium, accidens), and how classification depends on purposes and connotation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predication does not presuppose Classification
rubrics_metrics.description: Predication (using a general name to ascribe attributes) does not require that the speaker has formed or recognised a class; when we predicate a name we predicate only attributes, and class-membership may not come into view at all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if a general name creates a class when introduced, the logical act of predication concerns connoted attributes rather than explicit classification; do not conflate the act of naming/predicating with having an established classificatory scheme.

rubrics_metrics.name: General names often create classes but need not originate from them
rubrics_metrics.description: By every general name introduced we create a class (if there are things corresponding to its signification), but names are introduced either because we have a signification to express (predication) or because we find it convenient to create a class for regulation of mental operations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize two sources for class-names: (1) predicate-driven (to express attributes) and (2) classificatory convenience (to bind groups for a discipline, e.g., Cuvier's Plantigrades). Either way the name connotes attributes and denotes a class.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unlimited power to frame classes
rubrics_metrics.description: The power of framing classes is unlimited: take any attribute that some things have and others lack, and one may ground on that attribute a division of all things into two classes; there are as many classes as there are general names.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that many possible classifications exist; the mere possibility of naming or dividing does not by itself make a classification theoretically privileged or a 'real kind'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between kinds (real species) and accidental classes
rubrics_metrics.description: Some classes correspond to differences that extend to an indefinite (practically inexhaustible) number of properties and indicate a radical distinction (real Kinds); other classes differ only in a finite, enumerable set of properties (accidental differences).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat as 'Kinds' only those classes whose distinguishing attribute indexes an indefinite multitude of other peculiar properties (not merely a few superficial ones); superficial or finite differences (e.g., color) may be ignored unless the classificatory purpose demands them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aristotelian requirement for genus and species (essence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotelian logicians required that genus and species be of the 'essence' of the subject: genus and species must be Kinds (i.e., involve the indeterminate multitude of properties), not superficial accidental divisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In stricter taxonomies, only those divisions grounded in what was taken as the thing's essence count as genuine genera or species; bear in mind this is a theoretical stance and not a linguistic necessity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relativity of genus/species/differentia labels
rubrics_metrics.description: The terms genus, species, differentia, etc., are relative: the same predicate may be a genus with respect to one subject and a species with respect to another (e.g., 'animal' is genus relative to 'man' but species relative to 'substance').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing or constructing definitions, always specify the reference level or classificatory frame: a label like 'genus' depends on which subject and which larger or smaller classes are under consideration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Differentia
rubrics_metrics.description: Differentia is the part of the connotation of the species-name that distinguishes that species from all other species of the same genus; it is the surplus connotation that must be added to the genus to complete the species' connotation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentia may be ordinary or technical: it should be chosen according to the classificatory purpose; examples show 'rational' as differentia of man in ordinary use, but a different, technical differentia may be used in a scientific classification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentia may vary by classificatory purpose (technical connotation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The differentia for a species can change depending on the principle and purpose of the classification; words can acquire a special or technical connotation in a given scientific scheme that alters their connotation (e.g., Linnæan 'man' connoting dental characters rather than rationality).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When producing or evaluating classifications or definitions, state the intended classificatory purpose and any technical connotations to avoid ambiguity and misapplication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proprium (property) as necessary but non-connoted attribute
rubrics_metrics.description: A Proprium is an attribute which is not part of the connotation (definition) of the species-name but follows necessarily from some connoted attribute; it is inseparably attached to the species though not constitutive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two kinds of Proprium: (1) demonstrative (follows by demonstration from connoted attributes; e.g., opposite sides equal in a parallelogram) and (2) causal (follows as an effect of a connoted cause; e.g., capacity for language following from rationality). Use Proprium to capture necessary consequences of the defining attributes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accidens (accident) as non-essential, non-necessary attribute
rubrics_metrics.description: An Accidens is any attribute neither connoted by the name nor known to be necessarily connected to connoted attributes; accidents are divided into inseparable and separable accidents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inseparable accidents: universal in experience but not deductively necessary (e.g., blackness of crows—could be white crows). Separable accidents: present only in some individuals or times (e.g., color of Europeans, being born). When evaluating membership or definitions, distinguish between properties essential, necessary-consequent, and merely accidental.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infima species (proximate kind) comprehends properties of higher kinds
rubrics_metrics.description: Once the proximate (infima) species of an individual is ascertained, the properties common to that proximate kind necessarily include the common properties of every other real kind to which the individual can be referred (i.e., properties of superior genera are included).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In constructing definitions and deriving properties, start from the proximate species: its connoted and consequential properties subsume those of broader classes; ensure consistency when asserting what properties are entailed at different classificatory levels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Names acquire meaning by connotation and can be specialized
rubrics_metrics.description: What counts as the 'essence' or defining connotation of a name depends on how the name is used (ordinary vs technical use); names not otherwise connotative may acquire a special technical connotation for the purposes of a classification (e.g., whiteness defined by mixture of rays).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When producing definitions or evaluating terminology, document ordinary vs technical senses and any added connotative material that grounds the classification or definition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion for a class to be a real Kind
rubrics_metrics.description: A class is a real Kind (genus or species in the rigorous sense) if it is distinguished from all other classes by an indeterminate multitude of properties not derivable from one another (i.e., differences of kind rather than finite differences).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this criterion to test whether a proposed division captures a genuine ontological or deep classificatory distinction, rather than a superficial or pragmatic grouping; empirical investigation may convert putative accidents into necessary-consequent properties or vice versa.
